candidates.statement: Optical imaging uses light of a wide spectral range spanning from visible to near-infrared (NIR). Some 42 optical imaging drugs (e.g., indigo carmine) are dyes that can be directly visualized under white light, 43 whereas others contain a fluorescent moiety called a fluorophore that must be excited by specific 44 wavelengths of light before they emit light that can be visualized. Some optical imaging drugs target 45 cancers or the associated microenvironment through mechanisms including ligand binding to specific 46 receptors that are overexpressed by neoplastic cells or accumulation in tumors due to a unique 47 microenvironment attribute, such as lowered pH or increased proteolytic activity. In other 48 circumstances, optical imaging drugs delineate normal or abnormal anatomy by excretion in the urine 49 or bile or by physiological transit through the vascular system, lymphatic system, or gastrointestinal 50 tract. 51
candidates.context: products because of the loss of tactile perception and a more limited field of view with these 39 procedures. 40 Optical imaging during oncologic surgery aims to optimize tumor resection by enabling enhanced 53 tumor removal while minimizing resection of normal tissue. For primary solid tumors, complete 54 resection with negative tumor margins is often necessary for curative treatment. In this setting, 55 incomplete resection with positive margins or close margins (i.e., cancer cells within a certain distance 56 from the edge of resected tissue) is associated with poorer clinical outcomes . In clinical settings where 57 surgical debulking is indicated (e.g., metastatic ovarian cancer or high-grade glioma ), optical imaging– 58 guided surgery can aid the removal of an optimal amount of tumor tissue while minimizing resection of 59 normal tissue. 60

candidates.statement: For indication as an aid in tumor resection, the study should aim to show that detection and removal of 190 a tumor with optical imaging is significantly improved as compared with SOC procedures. Examples of 191 procedures to remove a tumor in which optical imaging may be employed are described below with 192 recommended endpoints. 193

candidates.statement: In clinical settings where the presence of positive margins directly affects patient management, the trial 197 should aim to show a reduction of the positive margin rate with use of the optical imaging drug as 198 compared with SOC resection. One such clinical setting is BCS, where positive margins may result in a 199 second surgery for the patient or a radiation therapy boost. 200

candidates.statement: Patient-level sensitivity and specificity are also recommended as endpoints of interest. In BCS, 214 histopathology results are generally reported by orientation or the anatomical location of a given 215 margin within the patient. Therefore, in the BCS setting, patient-level diagnostic performance should be 216 based on the imaging and histopathological results of all the margin orientations of the resection cavity. 217 The outermost face of tissue resected from a margin determines whether a corresponding margin 218 orientation is positive or negative. A method of converting tissue-level data to patient-level data should 219 be proposed and justified. 220

candidates.statement: • In an intrasubject trial design in which SOC resection of tumor occurs before optical imaging, for 399 the purpose of minimizing bias, subjects should be randomized to either an SOC arm or an SOC 400 plus optical imaging arm. Rationale should be provided for the proposed randomization ratio. All 401 eligible subjects receive the study drug before the start of surgery, and the surgeon should open the 402 randomization code only after the SOC procedure is complete to determine whether to perform 403 further surgery that relies on optical imaging. Alternatively, for the purpose of minimizing bias, 404 randomization to either a group receiving optical imaging drug followed by SOC and then optical 405 imaging or a group receiving placebo followed by SOC only may be considered. 406
candidates.context: In an intrasubject control design, randomization aims to minimize the potential of surgeons 395 underperforming using SOC methods (the first part of the procedure) due to knowledge of another 396 opportunity to intervene in the second part of the procedure using optical imaging. 397 In more complex settings where the surgeon needs to alternate between the optical imaging 408 technique and SOC, sponsors are encouraged to communicate with FDA early in product 409 development. 410

candidates.statement: • In an intrasubject trial design that employs an active comparator, the sequence of the imaging drug 412 administration can be randomized. However, if randomization of the imaging drug administration is 413 not feasible, randomizing the sequence of the imaging drug evaluation should be considered. The 414 order of administration or evaluation should be guided by the pharmacokinetics and 415 pharmacodynamics of both drugs. If none of these randomization approaches is feasible, a fixed 416 order of evaluation should be employed such that the investigational imaging drug is not given an 417 advantage. 418

When an important confounding factor exists 421 (e.g., longer procedure times with the investigational imaging technique possibly contributing to 422 improved detection of pathology), exploratory analysis to evaluate the impact of differential procedure 423 time between the two study arms is recommended. In such cases, a carefully planned statistical analysis 424 based on the confounding factor may provide additional information on the efficacy of the 425 investigational imaging drug. 426

candidates.statement: All subjects who are planned to be imaged with an investigational optical imaging drug should be 445 included in efficacy analyses. However, there may be intercurrent events or missing data that occur after 446 the start of study treatment and affect the interpretability of the study results. For example, not all 447 subjects in this intent-to-image set may have undergone image-guided surgery or may have reference 448 standard data collected or interpretable. In addition, there may be an incomplete administration of an 449 imaging drug due to a serious adverse reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis or other hypersensitivity reaction), 450 unevaluable imaging scan results, limitation of biopsy (e.g., imaging might inform about the need or 451 feasibility of a biopsy), or failed or uninterpretable histopathology evaluation for a reference standard. 452 Intercurrent events affect the interpretability of the treatment effect estimates. Missing data are data that 453 would be meaningful for the analysis of an estimand of an imaging drug effect but are not collected. 454

Intercurrent events and missing data 443 The primary strategy for handling intercurrent events and the primary method for imputing missing 456 data should be prespecified as part of the primary analysis for evaluating the optical imaging drug 457 effect on the primary efficacy endpoint. The intercurrent events handling should be based on event 458 type. The missing data approach should incorporate the reason for missingness. Optical imaging drug 459 sponsors are encouraged to prespecify one or more sensitivity analyses in addition to the primary 460 analysis to assess the robustness of the imaging drug effect estimate. 461

candidates.context: Sample size planning for a parallel-arm control design is generally based on the postulated effect size 465 of an investigational imaging drug relative to its comparator on the primary efficacy endpoint. With an 466 intrasubject control design, the effect size of interest is the average effect of adding an investigational 467 imaging drug to SOC for all subjects studied in the investigational arm. The sample size of the SOC- 468 alone arm depends on the proposed randomization ratio. 469 B. Safety Considerations 476

candidates.statement: • In phase 1 and phase 2 studies, the investigational optical imaging drug should not guide clinical 490 decisions and should not interfere with established practice standards. Following the demonstration 491 of acceptable performance of the investigational product, efficacy studies are designed to assess the 492 clinical performance and utility of the drug. 493
candidates.context: • Other potential optical imaging drug toxicities include photothermal effects and light-induced 486 generation of reactive oxygen species that may cause genotoxicity and mutagenicity. These risks 487 are evaluated during nonclinical studies. 488

candidates.statement: Labeling of optical imaging drugs can refer to a specific imaging device or can be device agnostic. A 527 wide range of imaging devices are available that use similar illumination strategies, light sources, 528 detectors, device architectures, and collection geometries, but some are developed for specific surgical 529 uses, and there may be significant differences among them. It is important that all devices used for a 530 specific intraoperative imaging use have adequate performance characteristics for its particular use. At 531 a minimum, imaging device characterization should address the following: 532
